achilles.excerpt: Achilles enters the Iliad by refusing to fight. The strongest warrior in the Achaean camp turns his strength against his own side, and an army begins to break around the absence of one man.

anubis.excerpt: Anubis guards a process. He wraps the dead, watches the burial ground, guides the deceased, and stands beside the balance where a heart is measured against the order it kept in life.

athena.excerpt: Athena’s first great image is an impossible birth: she comes from Zeus already armed. Greek tradition makes thought itself arrive with a spear, a shield, and a voice loud enough to shake the gods.

banshee.excerpt: The banshee does not kill the person whose death she foretells. She arrives as news before the news: a woman’s lament heard near a house, a road, a river, or the land of a family about to mourn.

baphomet.excerpt: Baphomet begins as a name in hostile mouths, not as an ancient goat-god waiting to be uncovered. Centuries pass before the name acquires the winged, horned body now recognized around the world.

hades.excerpt: Hades rules the dead; he does not tempt the living into sin, command a kingdom of fire, or wage war against Olympus. The Greek underworld is not Christian hell, and its king is not Satan in another costume.

lilith.excerpt: In the medieval tale, Adam and Lilith are made from the same earth. When he tells her that she must lie beneath him, she refuses. She says they were created equal, speaks the divine name, and flies away.

anansi.excerpt: In Akan storytelling, Anansi does not win because he is stronger than the animals around him. He wins by making a boast, setting a trap, or finding the one question no one else thought to ask.

ares.excerpt: In the Iliad, Ares changes sides, drives men into battle, and ends up wounded by a mortal with Athena’s help. Homer does not give him the dignity of a flawless war hero.

asclepius.excerpt: At Epidaurus, visitors did not only pray to Asclepius. They slept in his sanctuary and left inscriptions describing the cures they believed they had received.

ame-no-uzume.excerpt: When Amaterasu withdraws into the Heavenly Rock Cave, Ame-no-Uzume answers darkness with a performance that makes the assembled kami laugh.

anahita-ar-dvi-sura-anahita.excerpt: The Ābān Yašt addresses Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā as water with a name, a body, and the power to sustain life.

ark-of-the-covenant.excerpt: In Exodus, the ark is a portable acacia-wood chest placed beneath cherubim and described as the place from which Israel receives command.

baba-yaga.excerpt: In East Slavic folktales, the hut turns before Baba Yaga does: a house on chicken legs must be ordered to face the traveller who has reached its clearing.

medusa.excerpt: In Greek art, Medusa often looks straight out from the surface. Her face appears on temples, vessels, jewelry, and armor as an image meant to confront danger with danger.

persephone.excerpt: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Persephone is gathering flowers when the ground opens and Hades carries her away; only Hecate and Helios hear her cry.

gilgamesh.excerpt: When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh does not become wise at once. He keeps vigil over his friend, then sets out in terror because the death he has seen is his own future too.

mami-wata.excerpt: A late nineteenth-century image of a female snake charmer crossed commercial routes and was remade, in many African settings, into recognizably Mami Wata imagery.

quetzalcoatl.excerpt: At Teotihuacan, feathered-serpent reliefs move among shells across the temple facade. Centuries later, Mexica traditions use the Nahuatl name Quetzalcoatl for a feathered-serpent deity.
